items.claim: A privileged container has near-full host access, allowing an attacker to mount the host filesystem and gain a root shell.
items.body: When securityContext.privileged is true, the container can access host devices. The attacker lists devices with fdisk -l, mounts the host root partition, and chroots into it for a full host shell. Pod Security Standards and admission controllers should deny privileged containers.
items.disproof: Privileged containers are denied by policy, or the container runtime blocks device access.

sources.quote: Privileged Pods disable most security mechanisms and must be disallowed.
If a container runs with securityContext.privileged: true, it has near-full access to the host

items.claim: A mounted Docker socket inside a container lets an attacker spawn a privileged container with the host filesystem mounted, gaining host root.
items.body: If /var/run/docker.sock is available inside the container, the attacker runs docker -H unix:///var/run/docker.sock run -v /:/host --privileged ubuntu chroot /host bash. This creates a new privileged container with the entire host filesystem, granting full root access to the node.
items.disproof: The Docker socket is not mounted, or the container lacks permission to use it.

Container escape is the act of breaking out of a Docker/OCI container

items.claim: The cgroups release_agent technique escapes a container by writing a release_agent script that executes on the host when the cgroup empties.
items.body: The attacker mounts a cgroup, sets notify_on_release, writes a release_agent path pointing to a host-executable script, then triggers cgroup process exit. The kernel runs the script on the host, allowing command execution outside the container. This works on older kernels without seccomp/AppArmor restrictions.
items.disproof: Seccomp or AppArmor blocks cgroup manipulation, or the kernel is patched against this technique.

sources.quote: Containers are not a strong security boundary
